html:
A government drive after the Second World War to bring millions of migrants to Australia, at first from Britain and Europe and later from Asia.

The war had shown Australia to be a small population in a big land, open to attack. Prime Minister Ben Chifley set up a Department of Immigration in 1945, and its minister Arthur Calwell summed up the mood as "populate or perish".

The first waves were refugees and displaced persons from Europe, many from the Baltic states. Britons came cheaply on assisted passages and were nicknamed Ten Pound Poms. Then came Italians, Greeks, Dutch, Germans and Yugoslavs. Many worked on big projects such as the Snowy Mountains Scheme or in factories, and they changed Australian food, sport and city life.

At first the White Australia policy still kept Asians out. As it was dismantled up to 1973, the stream widened. Vietnamese refugees arrived from the late 1970s, followed by migrants from China, India and across Asia. Today almost a third of Australians were born overseas.
sum: A government drive after the Second World War to bring millions of migrants to Australia, at first from Britain and Europe and later from Asia.
